The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, and the weight cable sat snug on its drum among the gears. He tested each pin in the escapement and found every part sound. Then he leaned out through the louvres. Ice had formed on the face overnight, and its weight had bent both hands back against the numerals.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, and spoke of their cost and their safety. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, had stood in the square that morning and watched a man of seventy go up an iron ladder glazed with ice. She asked my grandfather to stay off the tower until someone younger could be trained to keep it. Someone raised the spring fair, three weeks off, and the vote went her way regardless.

No one younger came forward. On the night of the fair a storm took the power, and my grandfather struck a match at the kitchen table and lit the lamp, then sat beside it until late with the tower key in his lap, turning it over and over in his fingers.

In May he handed his notebook to me and asked me to keep it. The hands of the clock still stand at ten past four, bent a little toward the five, and the Harl bus leaves by the driver's watch now. Some mornings I stop in the square and think of that March day, when I might have offered to climb in his place, and of every hour the bell has missed since.

passage:
Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. In 2023 the park's warden, Petra Moss, asked Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, to find out why.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Moss blamed the grass crowding the flowers. Aldo Brisk, who has grazed his sheep on the slope for more than thirty years, blamed the late frosts, and his proof was the 1988 photograph he keeps in his kitchen: the slope blue to the crest in a summer, he says, when the last frost came in May. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks to keep the soil moist through the summer, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the sheltered plots held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The late frosts, it turned out, had been killing the flowers just as they opened.

The board met in October. A frost is beyond the reach of any vote, so the board has turned to Varga: seed from the sheltered plots will go to her greenhouses at Pellham, where she will raise seedlings to be planted out on the slope each June.

There will be cloths to cover them on any night the forecast turns cold. Whether that will be enough is far from clear. Plants raised under glass often struggle on an open hillside, and the late frosts have been coming more often, not less. Brisk, who was right all along, has taken to reading the thermometer by his door before he sleeps.
